stops.name: Bamburgh, the interdict and the exile
stops.campa: Word from Rome breaks the siege before spears do: the Pope, through the Bishop of Rochester, threatens England with interdict unless Arthur takes Guinevere back and accords with Lancelot. Arthur agrees, more from duty to his crown than any wish of his heart, and Lancelot rides the queen from Joyous Gard to Carlisle and gives her back to her husband with his own hands, kneeling to ask a pardon Gawain will not let the king grant. The queen is restored; Lancelot is not. He is given safe passage out of Britain instead, exile dressed as a settlement.

stops.name: Bayonne (Benwick), Gawain's pursuit
stops.campa: A hundred knights cross with Lancelot to his own inherited lands, which Malory calls Benwick and sets at Bayonne, and he divides the country among Bors, Hector and Lionel as new lords under him. Gawain will not let the matter rest in England and follows with Arthur's whole remaining host to besiege Benwick in turn, a war Lancelot fights half-heartedly, refusing again and again to kill the man he still loves despite everything. Twice Gawain forces a single combat by naming him traitor before both armies, and twice Lancelot beats him nearly to death and stops his own sword rather than finish it.

stops.name: Salisbury Plain, the field of Camlann
stops.campa: News that Mordred has seized the crown and the queen in Arthur's absence calls the king and Gawain home before Benwick falls, and Lancelot, still in France, is left out of the battle that ends everything. On Salisbury Plain, by the tradition this atlas already keeps for the Lady of the Lake, Arthur and Mordred kill each other in the day's last exchange, and the fellowship of the Round Table ends in a field of the dead. Lancelot lands days later with his own army, ready at last to fight for his king, and finds a battlefield already gone quiet and a war he came too late to join.

stops.name: Amesbury, the last meeting with the queen
stops.campa: He finds Guinevere at last not on a throne but veiled among the nuns of Amesbury, who took her in when the kingdom fell apart around her. She will not let him near her again in this life: she tells the sisters plainly, before he can speak for himself, that through her and Lancelot's love has been wrought all this war and the death of the noblest knights the world has known, her own lord among them. She asks only never to look on his face again, and to be let heal what is left of her soul in what days remain to her.
stops.quote: Through this man and me hath all this war been wrought, and the death of the most noblest knights of the world; for through our love that we have loved together is my most noble lord slain
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter IX

stops.name: Glastonbury, the death and burial of the queen
stops.campa: Lancelot takes the habit at the hermitage of the Archbishop of Canterbury near Glastonbury, where Sir Bedivere is already sheltering, and endures six years of penance there, a twelvemonth of them as an ordained priest singing mass. Then a vision comes three nights running and tells him to haste to Amesbury, for by the time he arrives the queen will be dead. She dies half an hour before he walks in, having prayed two days never to see his face again with worldly eyes. He and his eight fellows carry her the thirty miles back on foot, a hundred torches burning.

stops.name: Glastonbury, the death of Lancelot
stops.campa: After her burial he eats and drinks almost nothing, lying night and day grovelling on the tomb of Arthur and Guinevere, until he is dried and dwined away and his own fellows can hardly know him. Within six weeks he takes to his bed, asks his last rites against their protests, and asks that his body be carried to Joyous Gard, because he vowed once to be buried there. That night the hermit-bishop wakes the whole cell laughing: he has seen angels heave Lancelot up, and the gates of heaven opened against him. They find him dead, lying as though he smiled.
stops.quote: here was Sir Launcelot with me with mo angels than ever I saw men in one day. And I saw the angels heave up Sir Launcelot unto heaven, and the gates of heaven opened against him
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter XII (the hermit-bishop's vision on the night of Lancelot's death)

stops.name: Bamburgh (Joyous Gard), borne home for burial
stops.campa: The bishop and nine knights lay him in the same horse bier the queen was carried in and walk him north fifteen days, a hundred torches burning about him, to the one castle that was ever wholly his. At Joyous Gard they set his corpse in the body of the quire fifteen days more, his visage open and naked so that all folk may behold him. Into that service rides Sir Ector, who has searched England, Scotland and Wales seven years for his brother. He is buried there with great devotion, the map complete but for the one country he never entered.
stops.quote: thou were the courteoust knight that ever bare shield. And thou were the truest friend to thy lover that ever bestrad horse. And thou were the truest lover of a sinful man that ever loved woman. And thou were the kindest man that ever struck with sword
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XXI, Chapter XIII (Sir Ector's lament over the body of Lancelot at Joyous Gard)
